answer:
**A long history is useful only if you can find the parts relevant to this candidate.** A user may have 10,000 clicks spanning cooking, software, and travel. Averaging them all can blur current interests, while attending to every event for every candidate is expensive. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06978) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.03672) [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05639)

DIN makes history attention target-aware: when ranking a camera, photography-related events receive more weight than cooking events. DIEN additionally models how interests evolve through the sequence, helping distinguish old and recent patterns. Both become costly if applied naively to an unbounded history for hundreds of candidates.

**SIM separates finding evidence from interpreting it deeply.** A cheap first stage searches a relevant subsequence, perhaps by category or learned similarity. A richer second stage attends over that bounded subset. If 10,000 events are reduced to 100 plausible matches, the expensive interaction stage has far less work, though retrieval can miss useful older evidence.

Maintain compact session state, indexed long-term history, and cached candidate-independent summaries. Batch candidate scoring and count feature access and serialization in the 20 ms target; a warm model-only benchmark is insufficient. Evaluate quality as the subsequence budget changes, including users with diverse interests and useful old events. Recency is one clue, not proof that an old interest disappeared.

**Technical details and references.**

DIN attends to user-history items conditioned on the current candidate. DIEN models evolving interests with sequence dynamics and candidate-aware extraction. Applying either naively to 10,000 events for every candidate can exceed a 20ms budget. SIM first retrieves a relevant subsequence cheaply, then applies richer attention. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06978) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.03672) [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05639)

Store long-term history in an indexed representation, maintain compact recent/session state, and cache candidate-independent summaries. Retrieve a bounded number of category/semantic matches per candidate or candidate group, then batch fine scoring.

The 20ms target must include feature retrieval, serialization, and tail load, not only a warm GPU forward. Evaluate whether truncation/search misses older useful interests, and distinguish event recency from genuine preference changes. Measure quality versus history-search budget explicitly.
